summary.headline: Still about twice fair value: Rs 42.50 against a fair value near Rs 19.80, after four loss-making quarters
summary.text:
First Capital Holdings (CFVF.N0000) is a leveraged securities dealer, about 83% owned by the Janashakthi group: a government-securities primary dealer, corporate debt and equity trading, unit trusts (Rs 92.4bn managed), broking and advisory. Its profit follows interest rates. Falling yields gave EPS of Rs 22.15 in 2023/24 and Rs 11.58 in 2024/25; rising yields have reversed it. 2025/26 EPS was Rs 4.77 after Rs 1.05bn of VAT catch-up provisions, the last four quarters lost Rs 6.28 a share, and the six months to September 2026 lost Rs 1.21bn (EPS −Rs 2.99). NAV fell to Rs 16.42 from Rs 19.40 in March.

At Rs 42.50 (CSE close, 20 November 2026) it trades at 2.6x NAV, which needs a long-run return on equity of about 39%, its boom-year average. This full rebuild puts fair value at Rs 19.82 (was Rs 22.20): buy at up to Rs 16.85, strong buy under Rs 14.87. The fall comes from a lower long-run growth rate (4–6%, to fit what a 79% payout leaves to grow on), the house cost of equity (18.3%) and a residual income model that starts from today's −27% ROE. It still passes only two of the four business tests (heavy leverage, losses), so it stays in category 3, avoid for now. A fall in bond yields is the upside.

quality.reason: Very high returns in good years and generous dividends, but losses in 2021/22 and the last four quarters, and very heavy leverage.

tests.label: Return on equity of 15% or more
tests.note: Company ROE −14.1% (2021/22), 46.2%, 135.8%, 59.0%, 23.2% (2025/26); −27.2% over the twelve months to September 2026 (calculated). Passes over several years, but only because of the 2022–2025 fall in yields: a marginal pass.

tests.label: Net debt no more than equity
tests.note: Company's own debt to equity 12.30x at 30 Sep 2026 (7.07x in March). Excluding repos, overdraft, short-term and long-term loans and debentures were Rs 21.9bn against owners' equity of Rs 6.65bn. The primary dealer's capital ratio was 24.22% in March 2026 (not given for September).

tests.label: Steady profit: no loss in five years, no one-offs
tests.value: Losses in 2021/22 and the last four quarters
tests.note: EPS −1.50, 5.78, 22.15, 11.58, 4.77 over five years, then −2.99 in the half year; the second half of 2025/26 was also a loss (Rs 1.93bn for the year against Rs 3.26bn in the first half). 2025/26 also carried Rs 1.05bn of VAT catch-up provisions.

tests.label: Profit turns into cash and dividends
tests.note: Dividends of Rs 34.00 a share over 2021/22–2025/26 against EPS of Rs 42.78; Rs 2.84bn paid in cash in 2025/26. But 2025/26's Rs 7.00 was 147% of profit, nothing has been declared for 2026/27, and operating cash flow (−Rs 2.50bn in 2025/26) mostly reflects trading positions.

requiredReturn.betaBasis: Provisional. No local 5-year betas found (Simply Wall St 0.67 with no window stated; TradingView 1.39 is a 1-year beta). Refresh in January 2027.

valuation.note: Fair value weights the bear/base/bull averages of four methods 30/50/20 (about 1.2x NAV). No cash-flow DCF: this is a leveraged trading and financial-services group, so book value and return on equity drive the value. All four methods are computed by scripts/valuation.py.

highlights.title: Six months to September 2026 (unaudited)
highlights.text: Loss to shareholders Rs 1.21bn (EPS −Rs 2.99) against a profit of Rs 3.26bn a year earlier; second-quarter loss Rs 563mn (−Rs 1.39). Fair-value losses on securities were Rs 1.27bn and net trading income fell to Rs 0.73bn from Rs 3.95bn. A Rs 151mn tax credit softened the loss.

highlights.title: Where the losses came from
highlights.text: The primary dealer lost Rs 537mn (a Rs 1.69bn trading loss on government securities; net interest income Rs 687mn against Rs 988mn) and corporate debt and equity dealing lost Rs 765mn. Advisory earned Rs 69mn, broking Rs 12mn; asset management was about break-even with Rs 92.4bn under management.

highlights.title: Rates went the wrong way
highlights.text: The Central Bank raised its policy rate by 100 basis points in May 2026 because of Middle East-driven inflation; the 5-year bond yield rose to 11.12% from 9.84% in March. The same sensitivity works in reverse: a fall in yields would bring gains back quickly.

highlights.title: Bigger balance sheet, smaller equity
highlights.text: Total assets grew to Rs 101.0bn from Rs 74.2bn in six months, funded mainly by repos (Rs 69.3bn, from Rs 44.1bn) and short-term borrowings (Rs 12.1bn), while owners' equity fell to Rs 6.65bn. Debt to equity 12.3x (7.07x in March); interest cover 0.59x.

highlights.title: 2025/26 (audited)
highlights.text: Profit to shareholders Rs 1.93bn (EPS Rs 4.77) against Rs 4.69bn, after Rs 1.22bn of VAT on financial services, including Rs 296mn and Rs 751mn of provisions to settle past and later years at First Capital Limited. Dividend Rs 7.00 (147% of profit). ROE 23.2%.

models.name: Justified price to book
models.comment: NAV Rs 16.42 × (long-run ROE − growth) ÷ (cost of equity − growth): ROE 14% / 24% / 35%, growth 4% / 5% / 6%, cost of equity 19.8% / 18.3% / 16.8% (0.63x / 1.43x / 2.69x book).

models.name: P/E on normalised earnings
models.comment: Normalised EPS (NAV × long-run ROE) Rs 2.30 / 3.94 / 5.75 at 4.3x / 5.5x / 7.0x, at or below the justified 4.3x / 6.0x / 8.2x. Next year's EPS isn't used: the run-rate is a loss (−Rs 6.28 over twelve months, −Rs 5.56 on the latest quarter × 4), so the base case is a mid-cycle figure, not a forecast.

models.name: Dividend model
models.comment: Rs 0 / 1.00 / 3.00 next year, growing 4% / 5% / 6% (within the supported 2.9% / 4.9% / 7.2%) for five years; then normalised EPS with the stable payout 1 − g ÷ ROE (71% / 79% / 83%), at the cost of equity.

models.name: Residual income
models.comment: Book Rs 16.42; ROE moves from −27.2% (last twelve months, calculated) to 14% / 24% / 35% over three years, 79% payout, then excess returns grow at 4% / 5% / 6%. The weakest method because it charges for the losses still being made.

modelsNote: Four methods, all computed by scripts/valuation.py from modelInputs. Growth check: supported growth is 0% on 2025/26 alone (payout 147%) and 4.9% through the cycle (20.5% of profit kept × 24% ROE); long-run growth of 4% / 5% / 6% is within 2 points in every case. The long-run ROE is the key choice: 24% in the base case against a ten-year median of about 37%, because the high years came with big falls in bond yields. Ratio check (docs/ratio-ranges.md): beta 0.98 and cost of equity 18.3% are in range; long-run growth is below the 12.24% bond yield; ROE of 35% in the bull case and leverage of 12.3x are outside the normal ranges, which is the nature of a primary dealer.

scenarios.common: Cost of equity from the house formula: risk-free 8.24% (12.24% bond less a 4.0% default spread) + beta 0.98 × (4.2% + 6.08% country premium). Starting NAV Rs 16.42 (30 Sep 2026); 405m shares.

notes.disclaimer: These are estimates from the Annual Report 2025/26 and the interim reports to 30 June and 30 September 2026 (unaudited). The beta is provisional and the price is the CSE close of 20 November 2026, so check it before ordering. This is analysis, not personal financial advice.

Decision box.Verdict: Overpriced: about 114% above fair value of Rs 19.82.
Decision box.Downside / upside: Bear case about Rs 7.8; bull case about Rs 39.0, both below Rs 42.50.
Decision box.Confidence: Low: profit depends on interest-rate moves nobody can forecast.
Decision box.Margin of safety: Buy 15% below fair value (Rs 16.85), strong buy 25% below (Rs 14.87).

Business and moat.What it does: Primary dealer in government securities (First Capital Treasuries PLC, 89.44%), corporate debt and equity trading, unit trusts and private wealth (First Capital Asset Management, 98.70%; Rs 92.4bn under management), stockbroking (First Capital Equities, 100%), corporate advisory and trustee services.
Business and moat.Moat: Moderate: a large, long-established dealer and fund manager with strong ratings (group A+), but profit depends on market moves.
Business and moat.Parent: Janashakthi group holds about 83%; the public holds 16.98%.

Sri Lanka checks.Interest rates: The main driver: higher yields cause losses, falling yields big gains.
Sri Lanka checks.Tax: VAT on financial services cost Rs 1.22bn in 2025/26, including Rs 1.05bn of provisions to settle past and later years.
Sri Lanka checks.Regulation: The primary dealer refunded a Rs 216.8mn management fee (plus Rs 28.1mn interest) to follow Central Bank guidelines (interim note 4.1).
Sri Lanka checks.Liquidity: Only 17% of shares are in public hands; 500 shares (about Rs 21,250) trade easily.

What this analysis doesn't cover: Subsidiary reports (First Capital Treasuries' own accounts).
The primary dealer's capital ratio at September 2026 (not in the interim report).
The 2024/25 annual report, so last year's promises aren't checked; this year's are tracked against the half-year figures.
The annual report's investor-information page (p. 525) shows 2025/26 EPS Rs 6.47 and NAV Rs 21.10, which differ from the audited statements (Rs 4.77 and Rs 19.40); the audited figures are used.

fullText:
First Capital Holdings (CFVF.N0000) is a leveraged securities dealer, about 83% owned by the Janashakthi group: a government-securities primary dealer, corporate debt and equity trading, unit trusts (Rs 92.4bn managed), broking and advisory. Its profit follows interest rates. Falling yields gave EPS of Rs 22.15 in 2023/24 and Rs 11.58 in 2024/25; rising yields have reversed it. 2025/26 EPS was Rs 4.77 after Rs 1.05bn of VAT catch-up provisions, the last four quarters lost Rs 6.28 a share, and the six months to September 2026 lost Rs 1.21bn (EPS −Rs 2.99). NAV fell to Rs 16.42 from Rs 19.40 in March.

At Rs 42.50 (CSE close, 20 November 2026) it trades at 2.6x NAV, which needs a long-run return on equity of about 39%, its boom-year average. This full rebuild puts fair value at Rs 19.82 (was Rs 22.20): buy at up to Rs 16.85, strong buy under Rs 14.87. The fall comes from a lower long-run growth rate (4–6%, to fit what a 79% payout leaves to grow on), the house cost of equity (18.3%) and a residual income model that starts from today's −27% ROE. It still passes only two of the four business tests (heavy leverage, losses), so it stays in category 3, avoid for now. A fall in bond yields is the upside.

Valuation table (Rs per share)
Method | Bear | Base | Bull | Weighted
Justified price to book | 10.39 | 23.46 | 44.09 | 23.67
P/E on normalised earnings | 9.89 | 21.68 | 40.23 | 21.85
Dividend model | 5.12 | 16.30 | 37.82 | 17.25
Residual income | 5.64 | 16.16 | 33.69 | 16.51
Average | 7.76 | 19.40 | 38.96 | 19.82
Fair value Rs 19.82 (weights 30/50/20); buy Rs 16.85 (15% below), strong buy Rs 14.87 (25% below). Was Rs 22.20 / 18.90 / 16.60 on 13 November.

Why fair value fell (Rs 22.20 to Rs 19.82)
- Long-run growth cut to 4% / 5% / 6% from 5% / 6% / 7%: the company keeps only about 20% of its profit (Rs 34.00 of dividends on Rs 42.78 of EPS over five years), which supports about 5% growth at a 24% ROE.
- Cost of equity now from the house formula: 8.24% + beta 0.98 × 10.28% = 18.3% (19.8% / 16.8% bear and bull), close to the old hand-set 18.5%.
- Residual income now starts from the calculated ROE of the last twelve months, −27.2%, and recovers over three years; the old version assumed −5% / 5% / 15% for the next year.
- The dividend model now pays out 1 − g ÷ ROE of normalised earnings after five years (Damodaran's stable payout), and the P/E method uses 4.3x / 5.5x / 7.0x, at or below the justified P/E.

Assumptions
Cost of equity 19.8% / 18.3% / 16.8%; long-run ROE 14% / 24% / 35% (ten-year median about 37%, mostly from years of falling yields); long-run growth 4% / 5% / 6%; normalised EPS Rs 2.30 / 3.94 / 5.75 (NAV Rs 16.42 × ROE); next year's dividend Rs 0 / 1.00 / 3.00; residual income ROE path from −27% to the long-run level over three years, 79% payout.
Growth check: assumed 4% / 5% / 6%; supported 0% on 2025/26 alone (payout 147%), 2.9% / 4.9% / 7.2% through the cycle. All within 2 points.
Earnings run-rate: −Rs 6.28 over twelve months, −Rs 5.56 on the latest quarter × 4. The methods use mid-cycle earnings instead, because a loss run-rate can't be capitalised; the residual income model is where the current losses are charged.

Business tests: 2 of 4 passed. Returns pass over several years (five-year average about 50%) but only thanks to falling yields; debt fails (debt to equity 12.3x); steady profit fails (losses in 2021/22 and the last four quarters); cash passes (Rs 34 of dividends on Rs 43 of EPS over five years). Category 3, avoid for now (unchanged).

Management and plans
Management wants to make profit less dependent on bond trading, but the first half of 2026/27 shows the opposite so far: both trading arms lost money and the balance sheet grew on borrowed money. They plan to diversify income over the next 12–18 months, grow advisory and asset management and look at regional expansion. The Rs 3bn debenture was used to refinance short-term loans as promised; the balance-sheet promise was missed in the first half (equity −15%, debt to equity 12.3x).

Shareholders
Janashakthi PLC controls the company: 58.02% through eight accounts plus 24.99% through its subsidiary Janashakthi Insurance, 83.01% in all; the public holds 16.98% and the directors none. The September quarter was quiet: People's Leasing/Mr K.K. Shujeevan added 144,074 shares and Mr S.A. Thalangama (735,551) dropped out of the top 20.

500-share plan
200 shares up to Rs 19.80, 150 up to Rs 16.85, 150 up to Rs 14.85: about Rs 8,715 in total. Unrealistic for now: Rs 16.85 is about 60% below Rs 42.50 and far below 2026's low of Rs 38.00 (July–September). The share last traded near these levels in 2021/22, before the 2023–2025 boom. Another year of losses could pull the price down, but don't chase it.

What would change my view
Higher: Falling government-security yields (a policy rate cut), bringing trading gains back. ROE back above 25% for two or more years without more leverage. NAV growing again and dividends paid from current profit. Advisory, asset management and broking growing into a steady earnings base (management's 12–18 month diversification plan). Lower leverage or new capital that strengthens the primary dealer.
Lower: Further rate rises or a sharp rise in bond yields. Losses continuing into the second half of 2026/27, cutting NAV below Rs 15. More tax or VAT assessments. Funding stress in the repo market, or a fall in the primary dealer's capital ratio. A beta check in January that raises the cost of equity (each 1.5 points is worth about Rs 2–3 a share).
